We prove the two implications after setting up the three ingredients: (1) K/k is a cyclic Galois field extension of degree p with generator σ; (2) A is a central simple k-algebra of degree p, split by K; (3) for a central simple algebra of prime degree p, "division" is equivalent to "not split".

STEP 1: K/k is cyclic Galois of degree p, generated by σ.
Let f(T) = T^p - T - a ∈ k[T]. Since f is irreducible and x^p - x = a, the k-algebra homomorphism ev_x : k[T] → K, T ↦ x, is surjective (its image is k[x] = K) and its kernel is the maximal ideal (f). Hence K ≅ k[T]/(f) is a field and [K : k] = deg f = p, with k-basis 1, x, …, x^{p-1}.

Roots of f inside K: the prime field F_p lies in k. For each i ∈ {0,1,…,p-1} ⊂ F_p, using the characteristic-p binomial theorem ((u+v)^p = u^p + v^p) and Fermat's identity i^p = i in F_p,
  (x+i)^p - (x+i) = (x^p + i^p) - x - i = (x^p - x) + (i^p - i) = a + 0 = a.
So each x+i is a root of f. They are pairwise distinct: (x+i) - (x+j) = i - j ≠ 0 for 0 ≤ i < j ≤ p-1. Thus f has p distinct roots in K, all lying in K, and since deg f = p we have the factorisation f(T) = ∏_{i=0}^{p-1} (T - (x+i)) in K[T]. Moreover f'(T) = pT^{p-1} - 1 = -1 ≠ 0, so f is separable. Therefore K is the splitting field over k of a separable polynomial, i.e. K/k is Galois, and |Gal(K/k)| = [K:k] = p.

Existence and order of σ: since x+1 is another root of the minimal polynomial f of x over k, the assignment x ↦ x+1 extends (uniquely) to a k-embedding σ : K → K. Being a k-linear injection of the p-dimensional k-vector space K into itself, it is surjective, hence a k-automorphism. By induction σ^i(x) = x + i for 0 ≤ i ≤ p-1 (σ^{i+1}(x) = σ(x+i) = σ(x)+i = x+i+1, as σ fixes k ⊃ F_p). Hence σ^i ≠ id for 1 ≤ i ≤ p-1, and σ^p(x) = x + p = x + 0 = x since p = 0 in k, so σ^p = id on K = k(x). Thus σ has order p and, since |Gal(K/k)| = p, Gal(K/k) = ⟨σ⟩ ≅ Z/p. In particular K/k is a cyclic field extension of degree p with generator σ, exactly as required to apply the theory of cyclic algebras.

(The norm map N_{K/k} : K^× → k^× is the homomorphism N(y) = ∏_{i=0}^{p-1} σ^i(y); its image N_{K/k}(K^×) is a subgroup of k^×, so the quotient k^×/N_{K/k}(K^×) and the order of the class of b in it are well defined.)

STEP 2: A is a central simple k-algebra of degree p, split by K.
By the reference ref_22, part (i), applied to the cyclic Galois field extension K/k of degree n = p with generator σ and the element b ∈ k^×: the algebra (K/k, σ, b) with basis 1, u, …, u^{p-1} over K, relation u c = σ(c) u for all c ∈ K and u^p = b, is a central simple k-algebra of degree p; since K is a field, it is split by K (i.e. [A] lies in the relative Brauer group Br(K/k) = ker(Br(k) → Br(K))). Concretely dim_k A = [K:k]·p = p^2, so deg A = p. Note also that u is a unit of A, with inverse u^{p-1} b^{-1}, since u^p = b ∈ k^×.

STEP 3: for deg A = p, "A is a division algebra" ⇔ "A is not split".
By the Wedderburn structure theorem for central simple algebras, A ≅ M_r(D) for an integer r ≥ 1 and a central division k-algebra D, uniquely determined up to isomorphism, and deg A = r · deg D. Since deg A = p is prime, exactly one of the following holds:
 (a) r = 1 and deg D = p: then A ≅ D is a division algebra (no zero divisors);
 (b) deg D = 1 and r = p: then D = k and A ≅ M_p(k), which is NOT a division algebra, because p ≥ 2 and M_p(k) contains non-zero zero-divisors, e.g. the matrix units E_{11} ≠ 0 and E_{22} ≠ 0 satisfy E_{11}E_{22} = 0.
Case (b) is precisely the case in which A is split, i.e. [A] = 0 in Br(k). Hence: A is a division algebra ⇔ [A] ≠ 0 in Br(k) ⇔ A is not split. (Equivalently, exp(A) = 1 ⇔ [A] = 0 ⇔ A split, since the exponent of a central simple algebra is by definition the order of its Brauer class.)

STEP 4: exponent of A = order of b modulo norms, and this order is 1 or p.
By ref_23, applied to the cyclic extension K/k of degree n = p with generator σ and parameter b: exp(A) = exp((K/k, σ, b)) equals the order of the class of b in k^×/N_{K/k}(K^×).
By the proved lemma lemma_cyclic_norm_quotient_exponent_divides_degree (user eoinm), applied to the cyclic extension K/k of degree n = p, the quotient group k^×/N_{K/k}(K^×) has exponent dividing p. Since p is prime, every element of this quotient — in particular the class of b — has order exactly 1 or exactly p. Moreover the class of b has order 1 if and only if b ∈ N_{K/k}(K^×).

STEP 5: conclusion.
(⇐) Assume b ∉ N_{K/k}(K^×). By Step 4 the order of b in k^×/N_{K/k}(K^×) is not 1, hence is p. By ref_23, exp(A) = p ≠ 1, so [A] ≠ 0 in Br(k), i.e. A is not split. By Step 3, A is a division algebra. (This also matches the "in particular" clause of ref_23: order p gives a division algebra of exponent p.)
(⇒) Assume A is a division algebra. Suppose for contradiction that b ∈ N_{K/k}(K^×).
